title: Power Sets, Intervals & Products
goal: List power sets and count them, reason about `Pow` true/false claims, count intervals over ℤ vs ℝ, and build Cartesian products.
magic: `[` includes, `(` excludes; over ℤ `|[m, n]| = n − m + 1`.
A function: every input gets exactly one output.

blocks.title: 💡 Learn it, one idea at a time
The power set: the set of ALL subsets
blocks.summary: `Pow(X)` collects every subset of `X`, including `∅` and `X` itself. It has `2^|X|` elements.
blocks.picture: Pizza toppings {cheese, ham}. Every possible order: no toppings, cheese only, ham only, both. That menu of 4 choices is the power set.
blocks.official: `Pow(X) = {A : A ⊆ X}` and always `|Pow(X)| = 2^|X|` (Week 1, slide 31). Examples: `Pow(∅) = {∅}` (1 element), `Pow(Pow(∅)) = Pow({∅}) = {∅, {∅}}` (2 elements), `Pow({a}) = {∅, {a}}`. Note the type: `Pow(X)` is always a **set of sets**. Lecture exercise 1.4.4: `Σ = {a, b}` has subsets `∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}`, so `|Pow(Σ)| = 4`.

watch.answer: **8 subsets** (`2³ = 8`): list them by size so you don't miss any.

tries.why: `Pow({1}) = {∅, {1}}` has 2 elements, so its power set has 4.
`Pow(∅)` has 1 element, `Pow(Pow(∅))` has 2, and the next has `2² = 4`.

tries.q: Is `∅` an element of `Pow(X)` for every set `X`?

check.expr: all(frozenset() in Pow(A) for A in Pow(U))

trap.correct: Its elements are **subsets**: `∅, {1}, {2}, {1, 2}`. The plain numbers 1 and 2 are not elements.
trap.test: Every element of `Pow(X)` must itself be a set.

blocks.title: Power-set facts: which claims survive every set?
blocks.summary: `∅ ∈ Pow(A)` and `A ∈ Pow(A)` always. `Pow` works nicely with `∩` but not with `∪`.
blocks.picture: All the playlists you can make from songs in BOTH libraries = playlists you could make in each. But combining two libraries lets you make NEW mixed playlists that neither library alone allowed.
blocks.official: `X ∈ Pow(A) ⇔ X ⊆ A`. So `∅ ∈ Pow(A)` and `A ∈ Pow(A)`. `Pow(A ∩ B) = Pow(A) ∩ Pow(B)`, but only `Pow(A) ∪ Pow(B) ⊆ Pow(A ∪ B)` (they differ when a subset mixes elements of both). `Pow(A) ⊆ Pow(B) ⇔ A ⊆ B`. (Problem set 1, Q6 asks true/false questions of this kind.)

watch.q: True for all sets? `Pow(A ∪ B) = Pow(A) ∪ Pow(B)`.
steps: But `{1, 2}` is neither a subset of A nor of B.

tries.q: True for all sets? `Pow(A ∩ B) = Pow(A) ∩ Pow(B)`.

check.expr: all(Pow(A & B) == (Pow(A) & Pow(B)) for A in Pow(U) for B in Pow(U))

tries.why: Its only element is `A`, and `A ∈ Pow(A)`.

check.expr: all({A} <= Pow(A) for A in Pow(U))

tries.why: `∅` is a subset of every set, including `Pow(A)`.

check.expr: all(set() <= Pow(A) for A in Pow(U))

trap.tempting: `A ⊆ B` means the same as `A ∈ Pow(B)`, so `A ⊆ Pow(B)` too.
trap.correct: `A ∈ Pow(B)` ⇔ `A ⊆ B`. But `A ⊆ Pow(B)` would need every **element** of A to be a subset of B, a different claim.
trap.test: Check the type: elements of `Pow(B)` are sets.

blocks.magic: `X ∈ Pow(A) ⇔ X ⊆ A`. `Pow(A ∩ B) = Pow(A) ∩ Pow(B)`; not so for `∪`.

blocks.title: Intervals: brackets include, parentheses exclude, and the domain matters
blocks.summary: `[a, b]` includes both ends, `(a, b)` excludes both. Over ℤ an interval is finite: `|[m, n]| = n − m + 1`.
blocks.picture: A lift that stops at every floor from 2 to 6 inclusive stops 5 times. A ruler from 2 cm to 6 cm contains infinitely many points.
blocks.official: Intervals apply to any number type (Week 1, slide 35): `[a, b] = {x : a ≤ x ≤ b}`, `(a, b) = {x : a < x < b}`, plus half-open `[a, b)`, `(a, b]`. `[a, b] ⊇ [a, b), (a, b] ⊇ (a, b)`. `(a, a) = (a, a] = [a, a) = ∅`, but `[a, a] = {a}`. Over ℙ, ℕ, ℤ intervals are finite: `[m, n] = {m, m + 1, …, n}`, `|[m, n]| = n − m + 1`. Lecture exercise 1.3.10: `[−1, 1]` has 3 elements over ℤ but infinitely many over ℚ or ℝ.

watch.q: How many elements do `[−2, 2]`, `(0, 3)` and `[3, 10)` have over ℤ?
watch.answer: **5, 2, 7.** Over ℝ, all three are infinite.

tries.q: How many elements does `(1, 2)` have over ℤ? Over ℚ?
tries.why: No integer lies strictly between 1 and 2; infinitely many fractions do.

trap.correct: Both ends are included, so it's `n − m + 1`. (`[1, 3] = {1, 2, 3}`, 3 elements.)
trap.test: Test on a tiny interval like `[5, 5]`: the count must be 1.

blocks.title: Derived sets like `2ℤ` and `3ℤ + 1`
blocks.summary: `kℤ + r = {kx + r : x ∈ ℤ}`: the integers that leave remainder `r` when divided by `k`.
blocks.picture: A clock with 3 hours: every integer lands on 0, 1 or 2. `3ℤ + 1` is everything that lands on 1.
blocks.official: Week 1, slide 34: `2ℤ = {2x : x ∈ ℤ}` (the even numbers), `3ℤ + 1 = {3x + 1 : x ∈ ℤ}`. Also derived sets of positives: `ℕ>0 = ℤ>0 = {n ∈ ℤ : n ≥ 1} ⊂ ℚ>0 ⊂ ℝ>0`. To test `n ∈ 3ℤ + 1`, check `n mod 3 = 1`.

tries.why: Divisible by 2 and by 3 = divisible by `lcm(2, 3) = 6`.

check.expr: {n for n in range(-60, 61) if n % 2 == 0} & {n for n in range(-60, 61) if n % 3 == 0} == {n for n in range(-60, 61) if n % 6 == 0}

tries.why: A number has only one remainder mod 3.

trap.correct: `x` ranges over all of ℤ, so it also contains `…, −5, −2`.

blocks.title: Cartesian products: every ordered pair
blocks.summary: `S × T` pairs every element of S with every element of T. Order inside a pair matters. `|S × T| = |S| · |T|`.
blocks.picture: A menu with 3 mains and 2 drinks: every (main, drink) combo is one meal deal. `3 × 2 = 6` deals. (drink, main) would be a different listing.
blocks.official: `S × T ≝ {(s, t) : s ∈ S, t ∈ T}`, where `(s, t)` is an **ordered pair** (Week 1, slide 39). `S² = S × S`, `S³ = S × S × S`, and in general n-tuples. Facts: `∅ × S = ∅`; `|S × T| = |S| · |T|`; `|S₁ × … × Sₙ| = |S₁| · … · |Sₙ|`.

steps: Pair 1 with each letter: `(1, a), (1, b), (1, c)`.
Pair 2 with each letter: `(2, a), (2, b), (2, c)`.

tries.why: There is no second component to pair with.
Their first parts differ: `1` versus the pair `(1, 2)`. They carry the same information, though.

trap.tempting: `S × T` and `T × S` are the same set.
trap.correct: They contain the same **number** of pairs, but the pairs are flipped. Equal only if `S = T` or one of them is empty.
trap.test: Write one pair from each and compare the first components.

blocks.title: Functions as pairings: every input gets exactly one output
blocks.summary: `f : S → T` gives each element of S exactly one element of T. `f : x ↦ y` means `f(x) = y`.
blocks.picture: A seat assignment: every guest (S) gets exactly one seat (T). Two guests may share a table, but no guest gets two seats or none.
blocks.official: Week 1, slide 40: functions are a set-theoretic concept: `f : S → T` assigns to **every** element `s ∈ S` a **unique** element `t ∈ T`. `f : x ↦ y` means the same as `f(x) = y`. (Functions are covered properly in Week 3.) The number of functions from S to T is `|T|^|S|`, e.g. `2ⁿ` functions from an `n`-element set to `B = {0, 1}` (Week 2, slide 73).

watch.q: `S = {1, 2}`, `T = {a, b}`. Is the pairing `{(1, a), (1, b), (2, a)}` a function `S → T`?
steps: Every `s` must have exactly one partner.

tries.q: Same S, T. Is `{(1, a), (2, a)}` a function?
tries.why: Each input has exactly one output; sharing an output is fine.

tries.q: Same S, T. Is `{(1, b)}` a function `S → T`?

tries.why: Each of 3 inputs independently picks one of 2 outputs: `2³`.

trap.tempting: An input may have two outputs as long as the outputs are in T.
trap.correct: Each input has **exactly one** output. Different inputs may share an output.
trap.test: Scan the inputs: exactly one arrow leaves each.

items.why: Elements of a power set are sets; 2 is a number.

items.q: How many elements does `[−1, 1)` have over ℤ? Over ℝ?

blocks.sub: Problem set 1, Q6 style: true-for-all-sets claims about power sets and products. Original statements.

items.q: Which statements are true for **all** sets `A`, `B`?
items.why: (1): `∅ ⊆ A`. (2): `X ⊆ A ∩ B` ⇔ `X ⊆ A` and `X ⊆ B`. (3) fails for `A = {1}, B = {2}`. (4): subsets of A are subsets of B exactly when `A ⊆ B`.

exprs: all(frozenset() in Pow(A) for A in Pow(U))
all(Pow(A & B) == (Pow(A) & Pow(B)) for A in Pow(U) for B in Pow(U))
all(Pow(A | B) == (Pow(A) | Pow(B)) for A in Pow(U) for B in Pow(U))
all((Pow(A) <= Pow(B)) == (A <= B) for A in Pow(U) for B in Pow(U))

check.expr: all(len(cart(Pow(A), Pow(A))) == 4**len(A) for A in Pow(U))

items.q: True or false: `(A × B) ∩ (A × C) = A × (B ∩ C)` for all sets.
items.why: A pair `(a, x)` is in both products exactly when `a ∈ A` and `x ∈ B` and `x ∈ C`.

check.expr: all((cart(A, B) & cart(A, C)) == cart(A, B & C) for A in Pow(U) for B in Pow(U) for C in Pow(U))

items.q: `A = {1}`, `B = {2}`, `C = {3}`. Is `A × (B × C) = (A × B) × C`? Is there a one-to-one matching between them?
items.a: **Not equal:** `(1, (2, 3)) ≠ ((1, 2), 3)`. **But yes, a bijection:** `(a, (b, c)) ↦ ((a, b), c)` matches them perfectly (both have `|A||B||C|` elements).
items.why: Equal only in the degenerate case where one of the sets is empty (both sides are then `∅`).
If both are non-empty and `a ∈ A \ B`, then any `(a, b)` is in `A × B` but not in `B × A`.

check.expr: all((cart(A, B) == cart(B, A)) == (A == B or not A or not B) for A in Pow(U) for B in Pow(U))

items.q: How many elements does `Pow({1, 2}) \ Pow({1})` have? List them.
How many subsets of `{1, …, 10}` contain the element 1?
items.why: Fix 1 in; each of the other 9 elements is in or out: `2⁹`.

check.expr: sum(1 for S in Pow(range(1, 11)) if 1 in S)

lines: `Pow(∅) = {∅}`, `Pow({a}) = {∅, {a}}`, sizes double with each new element.
`Pow(A ∩ B) = Pow(A) ∩ Pow(B)`; `Pow(A) ∪ Pow(B) ⊆ Pow(A ∪ B)` only.
Intervals: finite over ℤ, infinite over ℚ/ℝ (unless empty or a single point).
Products: order matters; `(a, (b, c)) ≠ ((a, b), c)` but they match one-to-one.
